claims.text: Reducing atomic disorder in high-entropy alloys enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling increases the superconducting transition temperature.
The initial alloy is equiatomic and highly disordered.
Controlled thermal annealing can reduce atomic disorder while maintaining the alloy's overall composition.
Controlled measurement environments can avoid extrinsic effects so that atomic disorder is the only relevant varying factor.
Atomic disorder gives rise to local lattice distortions.
Structural analysis can quantify local lattice distortions associated with atomic disorder.
High atomic disorder increases electron scattering.
High atomic disorder disrupts spatially uniform electron–phonon coupling.
Uniform electron–phonon coupling is necessary for robust Cooper-pair formation in the proposed alloy regime.
Annealing smooths local variations in electron–phonon coupling by reducing disorder.
Annealed samples with reduced disorder will exhibit a higher superconducting transition temperature than the untreated baseline.
Annealed samples with reduced disorder will exhibit a sharper superconducting transition than the untreated baseline.
The proposed mechanism is most relevant when electron–phonon coupling is the primary pairing mechanism.
Secondary-phase formation or impurity scattering can obscure the effect of disorder reduction on superconductivity.
The magnitude of the transition-temperature increase and its relationship to disorder reduction may vary with alloy composition.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening and transmission electron microscopy can serve as structural-disorder metrics for the comparison.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase and sharpening of the transition temperature, or failure of transition-temperature changes to correlate with reduced disorder, would falsify the hypothesis.
